title: Connectivity Controls Variational Accessibility in Symmetry-Preserving Quantum Circuits
abstract: Designing expressive quantum circuits for the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) is a central challenge in simulating interacting many-body systems. Even symmetry-preserving (SP) circuits need not access the full many-body symmetry sector. We demonstrate this explicitly for the spin-$1/2$ XXZ and Hubbard models, where Hamiltonian-inspired nearest-neighbor (NN) SP circuits generate restricted dynamical Lie algebras (DLAs). While these restricted manifolds can accurately represent the ground state near the free-fermion limits, $J_z=0$ for XXZ and $U=0$ for Hubbard, interactions expose inaccessible many-body directions and severely limit VQE performance even at large circuit depth. Remarkably, a minimal modification of the generator connectivity can reconstruct the full orthogonal DLA within all relevant symmetry sectors studied in this work. For XXZ model, the addition of {\it only} one SP next-to-NN single-excitation connection triggers this dramatic reconstruction, whereas the Hubbard case requires a SP correlated double-excitation;--showing that the relevant connectivity can extend from the spatial lattice to many-body configuration space. This reconstruction enlarges the tangent space and accessibility of the energy-lowering Hamiltonian direction, leading to near-unit ground-state fidelity in VQE simulations. Our results establish a direct link between generator connectivity and variational accessibility and suggest a broader circuit-design principle: identify minimal symmetry-preserving generators that enlarge the accessible many-body space rather than increasing circuit depth alone. This perspective may have broader relevance for quantum many-body simulation at the interface of condensed-matter physics and quantum computing.
summary: This work investigates how the connectivity of quantum circuit generators limits the variational space available to VQE algorithms for models like the Hubbard and XXZ Hamiltonians. The authors prove that simply increasing circuit depth is insufficient; instead, adding specific, minimal long-range or correlated gates is necessary to reconstruct the full symmetry-preserving Lie algebra. This establishes generator connectivity as the key determinant of variational accessibility in quantum simulation.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of designing expressive quantum circuits for the Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) when simulating interacting many-body systems.
main_result: The variational accessibility of the circuit is fundamentally controlled by the generator connectivity, not just the circuit depth; minimal additions of specific symmetry-preserving generators can reconstruct the full dynamical Lie algebra, leading to high VQE fidelity.
method: The authors analyze the Dynamical Lie Algebra (DLA) generated by ansatz operators and correlate its dimension and the resulting tangent-space rank ($r_T$) with VQE performance metrics like ground-state fidelity and energy error.
model_or_system: The study focuses on spin-1/2 XXZ and Hubbard models, which are canonical models for strongly correlated electrons, studied within fixed symmetry sectors.
key_observables: Variational accessibility (measured by $r_T$ and Hamiltonian alignment $A_H$), ground-state fidelity ($F$), and energy error ($\Delta E$).
important_parameters: Interaction strengths ($J_z$ for XXZ, $U/t$ for Hubbard), and the type of generator connectivity (Nearest-Neighbor vs. Next-to-Nearest-Neighbor or correlated double-excitation).
main_assumptions: The analysis is performed within fixed, conserved symmetry sectors of the Hamiltonians.
figures_summary: Figures compare VQE performance metrics ($r_T$, $A_H$, $\Delta E$, $F$) as a function of circuit depth and system parameters, demonstrating the dramatic improvement upon adding specific long-range or correlated gates.
paper_structure: The paper establishes a link between connectivity and accessibility by comparing NN-only circuits to minimally augmented circuits (NN+1 or NN+d) for both the XXZ and Hubbard models, showing algebraic reconstruction leads to physical performance gains.
why_interesting: It provides a concrete, actionable principle for designing quantum circuits for condensed matter simulations, suggesting that algebraic structure (connectivity) is a more fundamental resource than simple circuit depth.
